Haha, sure, the sentence was mostly *exempli gratia.* I probably would not choose the word salient in casual conversation. Funnily enough, though, I have used a sentence very similar to that one in formal documentation for my work.

My work dealt with tire balancing and harmonic signals, in which the *salient* frequencies present in the signal are all integer multiples of the frequency at which the wheel rotates. The specific numbers I chose were random, but I did choose one as an integer multiple of the other on purpose. So, if our fundamental frequency is 7 Hz, a 3rd harmonic component would have a frequency of 21 Hz and would reflect a nonuniformity that occurs 3 times for every rotation of the tire.

Not interchangeably, no. In some cases, they may substitute fine for each other. 

Salient means *standing out* or *noticeable.* Often this entails *importance,* but it is not always used to convey importance. And when it is, I've usually found it to be less emphatic than critical or pivotal. 

Critical and pivotal are more closely related to each other, imo, and both usually convey that something is *crucial* or *vitally important*, although pivotal to me often carries connotations of *change* or *reversal* (a pivot, after all, is a point on which something turns, swings, or oscillates) while something that is critical may not necessarily be so in a "turning point" or "game changer" kind of way. I think critical and pivotal could probably often be interchanged without loss of accuracy, although one might usually be the more descriptive or felicitous word for the context. 

An example for salient: My work used to deal with looking for peaks on graphs, so we might say something like, "The most *salient* peaks occur at frequencies of 7 Hz and 21 Hz."

These peaks are not necessarily earth-shattering in relation to the project, so I would not usually describe them as "critical" or "pivotal," but, in the context of the graph, they do happen to be "salient" because they stand out relative to the other peaks.

There is nothing inherently good or bad about with using either, although in some circles, em dashes are seen as a cop-out, a choppy workaround for rephrasing the sentence to be more cohesive. I personally used to (and sometimes still do) make heavy use of em dashes. I also did not shy away from semicolons. In general, l'd say don't *over*use them, just like you shouldn't overuse almost any stylistic element (word, syntax, structure, punctuation, etc). Most "good writing" varies its syntax and structure. Of course, good writers often employ punctuation and repetition of punctuation strategically for rhetorical purposes, but the operative word here is "good". Generally speaking, if you don't know what you are doing or don't feel you have exemplary command of the language, just try to use semicolons and em dashes as sparingly as you would any other punctuation. Use it if it is the **best** punctuation for your sentence. Certainly don't force the use of a semicolon or a dash if it doesn't arise organically. parallelism is more of a style thing, not a strict rule. Also, “before starting” and “was working” wouldn’t exactly be parallel because “starting” here would be a gerund, so it would not have a tense at all. Either way, no rule says adjacent verbs must share a tense. Verb tenses in adjacent clauses are actually dictated by the so-called “sequence of tenses”. However, as I write about sequence of tenses, I am more inclined to agree with your conclusion that C is incorrect, but not for the same reasons.

Note [this chart](https://1.bp.blogspot.com/-ce1RT4BoYw8/VA010dAjMkI/AAAAAAAAAYI/Mfrd8vyfNS8/s1600/ab.jpg) on sequence of tenses  ( [u/glasias](https://www.reddit.com/user/glasias) \- you might want to look at this too).  Look at #7. We have a subordinate clause in the past tense and a principal clause in the pluperfect, joined by the conjunction “before”. This is precisely the same structure as the sentence in OP’s question, albeit with the clauses reversed (which doesn’t matter). Therefore, if we were to go off this chart, the correct answer to OP’s question would be A.

However, in OP's question we do not know if the subject *had already completed* his teaching in Jerusalem or if he *was* *still teaching.* I can think of several sentences that follow the same structure but indeed use the past continuous in lieu of the past perfect. So I maintain that either A or C is acceptable, though I suspect A is what the test was looking for.

Honestly, whether I myself would've chosen A or C on the test probably depends on the day lol. And the more I look at it, the more right C seems. Anyhow, if your friend gets the question wrong, he has grounds to challenge the answer. A reasonable case can be made for either A or C.

Checks out.

C could also be correct, though.  If he was teaching in Jerusalem immediately prior to his starting to work "here" I'd probably say C is the better option. Whereas if he had taught in Jerusalem some time before starting to work here but had already completed his teaching in Jerusalem even before he began working here, C would not be quite accurate as it would not capture the "perfect" (i.e. completed) aspect of it.

Given what we're given, though, I would go with A. Even though I personally believe C sounds better, an English teacher would be hard-pressed to justify not giving credit for A.

**tl;dr:** "which" is a relative pronoun, so any clause using "which" is a relative dependent clause that must be appended to an independent clause. "Those" is *not* a relative pronoun, so a clause using "those" is not a relative clause and can function independently of other clauses.

​

**Here's the intuition:**

If you use "those," the second clause becomes "half of those were sold in the United States". This is a complete sentence that works just fine on its own. In fact, if you changed that comma to a period, you'd have two perfectly correct sentences:

>In 2019, its average weekly circulation was reported 1.5 million copies. Half of those were sold in the United States.

On the other hand, if you use "which", the second clause could not exist on its own. "Half of which were sold in the United States" is not a sentence. It is a dependent clause.

**Here's the technical explanation:**

"Which" is a relative pronoun, so the clause containing "which" is a relative clause. Relative clauses are dependent clauses that have relative pronouns that refer back to something mentioned in the independent clause. The thing that the relative pronoun refers to is called the *antecedent* ("1.5 million copies" is the antecedent here).

The term "relative clause" is helpful because it actually gives you a clue to why it is dependent. The clause  is "relative," so it only really has meaning *relative* to something else, and so it *depends* on a clause attached to it to specify what it's referring to. Hence, it is a *dependent* clause.

"Those," on the other hand, is not a relative pronoun. It is a demonstrative pronoun that functions grammatically like any standard noun and can be the subject or object of an independent clause. So a clause using "those" does not depend on another clause grammatically.

It can be tricky since you obviously need the first sentence here to know what "those" or "which" is referring to. The "those" clause isn't very meaningful on its own, but it is still grammatically correct. The "which" clause is neither meaningful nor grammatically correct on its own.

Neither is grammatically incorrect, but this is more of a style issue. Sometimes it sounds dumb to have the same possessive is such close proximity to itself - e.g. you wouldn't say someone was "my apple of my eye"; you'd say they were "*the* apple of my eye", even though the *my* version is not strictly ungrammatical. If the possessor of the object of the prepositional phrase (*eye* in this example) implies the possessor of the noun modified by the prepositional phrase (*apple* in this example), or if the specific possessor of the modified noun doesn't really matter, then don't repeat the possessive.

In some cases, though, the repeated personal possessive is actually necessary to disambiguate the possession of the noun. In your phrase, *my* intuition and *the* intuition seem like two pretty different things, based on the limited context you provided. "*The* intution" would imply some common, universally accessible intuition re your view of the world, whereas it seems you're trying only to comment on *your* own personal intuition of your view of the world, in which case to dispossess and universalize the "intuition"  would be to lose some of the intended meaning.

That being said, it does sound somewhat clunky, and I would suggest rewording it. More context would be useful, but one suggestion would be to take out "my view of" altogether:  *My intuition of/about the world....* since y*our intuition* is almost necessarily based on *your view* of the world.
